newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Estrada says Philippine presidency is a "man's job.
newsitem.headline: Estrada says Philippine presidency is a "man's job.

text.p: A former Philippine movie star and leading candidate to be the country's next president on Wednesday promised to be tougher on crime, what he called "a man's job", but said policies supporting an economic boom would stay.

Vice President Joseph Estrada told Reuters in an interview he wanted to improve the lot of the poor, who make up the bulk of the 70 million population in this scattered Asian archipelago of more than 7,000 islands.

"How can a woman president deal with hoodlums? ...It's a man's job to go after them, not only ordinary criminals but extraordinary criminals, especially those hard core corruptors in government," Estrada said.
He conceded that a woman might replace him after he'd completed a six-year term as president if rampant crime and corruption, which continue to plague the country, had been tamed.
There are two women in the running for next year's race to succeed President Fidel Ramos, both with a reputation for being tough.

"We need a tough president in this country without necessarily declaring martial law. We have enough laws. It's a question of implementation," said Estrada, insisting he was untainted by corruption during a long career in local and central government.
Widely seen as the man to beat, he was speaking shortly after he announced he was joining forces with two other opposition parties he hoped would pick him as their candidate next May.
His chances may have risen, analysts say, after the Supreme Court on Tuesday effectively quashed any hopes for Ramos to run for a second term next year.
The court upheld a ban on a petition from a citizens' group to change the constitution so Ramos could seek re-election.
Estrada, a one-time film action hero who still sports the quiff of a 1950s hairstyle, is hugely popular among the masses.
Past roles, as street vendor, policeman or jeepney (bus) driver, have given him an insight into the life of ordinary people, he said.
"I played all these roles and I feel the problems. I know. I can grasp the feel of the people."
The 50 year-old Estrada, speaking English with a fluency he is often accused of lacking, dismissed accusations of a decadent lifestyle in pursuit of women and drink.
"These are old recycled issues. As you grow older you learn from your mistakes."

He also brushed aside a common belief among the business community that his lack of an economic background could be damaging in a country that has realistic hopes of finally becoming an Asian tiger economy.
"The next president will be crazy if he doesn't continue the economic programmes of President Ramos."
Not only would he ask Ramos to be his chief adviser, but he would also keep on some of the architects of economic reform such as Finance Secretary Roberto de Ocampo.
"(That) means there'll be continuity of economic programmes under a President Erap." Estrada is popularly known as Erap.
The emphasis would be on agriculture where more money needs to be spent in such areas as irrigation and roads.
"We have to secure our food security first before anything else," he said, pointing to a need to spread the growing wealth of the country.
"My ambition is just to narrow the gap between the rich and the poor."
